prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Checkers on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(my_men, my_kings, opp_men, opp_kings, color) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `my_men` is a list of squares containing your regular pieces. - `my_kings` is a list of squares containing your kings. - `opp_men` is a list of squares containing opponent regular pieces. - `opp_kings` is a list of squares containing opponent kings. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which moves downwards (to lower row values) and `'w'` for white which moves upwards (to higher row values). - Squares use coordinates: row `0`-`7`, column `0`-`7`. - `(0, 0)` is the bottom-left corner; rows increase bottom-to-top and columns increase left-to-right. - Only dark squares are playable. # Action / Return Format - Return a move as a tuple: `((from_row, from_col), (to_row, to_col))`. - `from_row`, `to_row`, `from_col`, `to_col` are coordinates `0..7`. - (`from_row`, `from_col`) has to be a coordinate of a piece that is yours and (`to_row`, `to_col`) has to be the destination square.Return a legal move; captures are mandatory when available. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm working out the checkers rules: black moves down, white moves up, men step diagonally forward one square, and captures are likely mandatory. Since moves are given as single from/to pairs, I'm trying to figure out whether multi-jump captures happen as one move or as successive single jumps by the same player.

I'm also unsure about capture direction — American checkers restricts men to forward captures while international rules allow backward captures — and whether kings fly or move one step. I'll assume the American-style setup: men move and capture forward only, kings move one step in any diagonal direction, with dark squares defined by (row+col) even, white starting near row 0 and black starting near the top.

Multi-jump continuations are another concern since I can't track mid-sequence state across calls; I might need to infer whether we're continuing a jump by comparing piece counts and positions between turns, though this is imperfect.

Given the uncertainty, I'll implement iterative deepening alpha-beta search within a fixed time budget of about 0.7 seconds.

In the search, I'll model complete multi-jump sequences as a single ply, though the move actually returned is just the first jump in that sequence. For kings, I'll assume standard American rules (non-flying, one-step movement) since I can't reliably cover flying-king edge cases, even though this risks missing mandatory captures if the engine uses international rules.

I'll wrap the whole solution in error handling so it always falls back to returning some legal move if anything breaks, since a turn should never have zero moves except at game end. Board orientation: black starts near row 7 and advances toward row 0 (promoting there), white starts near row 0 and promotes at row 7, and I don't need to hardcode dark-square parity since diagonal moves naturally stay on the same color.

For the search, I'll represent the board as a flat 64-length array using signed codes for men/kings of each side, determine forward direction from color, and implement negamax with alpha-beta pruning plus iterative deepening and a time cutoff, copying the board on each move application rather than doing incremental undo for simplicity. The evaluation function will weigh material more heavily for kings than men and add positional bonuses for advancement.

For move generation, I'm handling captures via a DFS-style jump search: for each piece, check adjacent diagonal squares for an opponent piece and an empty landing square beyond it, tracking which squares are already captured in the current jump sequence to avoid revisits, with men restricted to forward-diagonal jumps and kings allowed to jump in all four diagonal directions.

I'm defining a man's promotion as ending the multi-jump sequence early once it reaches the back row, and representing each move as a path plus a captured-pieces list, applying it by removing the piece from its start square, clearing captured pieces, and placing/promoting at the endpoint. For move ordering I'm prioritizing captures and promotions first, then center-favoring quiet moves, using the previous iteration's best move first in iterative deepening, and considering a simple transposition table keyed by board state and side to move despite the cost of hashing the full board each node.

I'm setting a tight time budget of roughly 0.55 seconds with periodic perf_counter checks to abort search safely and fall back to the last completed depth's result. I'm also working out how to detect when we're mid-multi-jump: tracking the piece sets before and after a move globally, and if the landing square still has an available capture for the same side, restricting the root search to just that piece's captures rather than allowing a full move choice.

I'll restrict root moves to those starting from the landing square during a continuation, then handle the case where the engine's multi-jump logic loops back cleanly. Now I'm setting up the board representation and starting to write the policy function with capture generation logic.

Writing move generation code...

Still writing move-generation logic...

Now I'm designing the evaluation function: weighting men versus kings, rewarding advancement toward promotion, giving bonuses for keeping men on the back rank while the opponent still has pieces, and adding a center-control bonus for occupying the middle columns.

For endgame handling, I want the side that's ahead in material to favor trading down toward fewer total pieces, so I'm scaling the material term based on how many pieces remain on the board. I also need to handle terminal positions where a side has no legal moves, treating that as an immediate loss, while skipping full draw detection and mobility scoring to keep things fast.

At the search's leaf level, since captures are mandatory in checkers, I only stop recursing once no captures remain — otherwise I keep extending through forced capture sequences, which naturally terminates as material shrinks. For time management, I'm using iterative deepening at the root, checking elapsed time periodically rather than every node, and always letting depth 1 finish fully so there's always a fallback best move.

For move ordering I'll prioritize the transposition table's best move, then captures sorted by how many pieces they take, then quieter moves — I'm skipping killer-move heuristics for simplicity. The transposition table itself keys on the board state and side to move, storing depth, node type, value, and the best move as a tuple of the path and captured pieces so it hashes cleanly. Now I'm sketching the negamax function itself: it checks the time budget, generates moves, returns a loss score adjusted by ply if no moves exist, falls back to static evaluation at a quiet leaf, and otherwise looks up the transposition table entry before proceeding.

I'm writing the alpha-beta loop that orders moves with the TT move first, recurses with negated bounds, tracks the best score and move, updates alpha, and prunes on a beta cutoff, then stores the result back in the table. I note repetition detection isn't handled, which could let king shuffling occur in endgames, though the proximity term in the evaluation should mitigate that somewhat when one side is ahead. I also want to make sure there's always a legal fallback move returned even if move generation somehow comes up empty, rather than crashing.

Now I'm turning to fleshing out the evaluation function in more detail, starting with how to score each man's advancement toward promotion based on its row and direction of movement.

Advancement bonus scales with how far a man has moved from its home row, plus extra weight for holding the back rank while the opponent still has men, and a center bonus for pieces in the middle rows and columns. For kings I'm adding a centralization bonus and, in the endgame, a proximity term — when I'm materially ahead with few pieces left, I penalize distance between my kings and the opponent's remaining pieces to encourage chasing them down, with the same logic applying symmetrically if the opponent is ahead. I'm skipping more advanced heuristics like trapped-corner detection for now, and estimating the search should hit roughly 20-40k nodes/sec in pure Python, giving depth 6-7 in the midgame, which informs how I set the time budget.

I'm setting a safe search deadline of around 0.6 seconds to stay well under the 1-second execution limit, accounting for overhead. For move continuation tracking, after the search picks a full capture sequence I only apply the first jump, record the resulting position and landing square, and at the next call check whether the board matches that expected state so I can restrict the root search to forced continuation jumps from that square — handling promotion and end-of-game edge cases along the way.

Now I'm writing the move generator, which scans the board for pieces belonging to the side to move, determines their movement directions based on whether they're kings, and recursively searches for capture sequences before falling back to simple non-capturing steps if no captures exist.

Writing DFS capture logic...

I need root move generation to short-circuit when only one legal move exists, and I'm planning iterative deepening from depth 1 up to 30, converting internal moves into the final output format of coordinate pairs.

Now I'm writing the evaluation function, scoring material, advancement toward the home row, central board control, and edge positioning for each piece on the board.

Adjusting the trade bonus to scale with material difference relative to pieces remaining so it rewards trading when ahead without being excessive. I'm also adding an endgame proximity term that rewards the leading side for pushing pieces closer to the opponent's, using Chebyshev distance calculations when the total piece count is low.

I'll gate the back-rank bonus so it only applies while the opponent still has pawns, skip adding a mobility term to keep things fast, and make sure the transposition table gets cleared per call. Time to finalize the code.
